facts.raw_span: a 2‐day history of right lower‐extremity numbness and pain
manual muscle testing of the right tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus was 3/5
gastrocnemius and flexor hallucis longus were 4/5
deep‐tendon reflexes were normal
Straight‐leg‐raising was positive at 70 degrees
the femoral‐nerve stretch test was negative
Plain radiographs showed degenerative scoliosis at L5–S1
Lumbar MRI demonstrated a right‐sided disc herniation at L5–S1
Initial peroneal‐nerve conduction studies revealed a motor conduction velocity of 51.5 m/s
Ankle‐brachial indices were decreased (0.78 on the right, 0.73 on the left)
lower‐extremity arteriography showed no significant vascular lesions
right foot drop (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, flexor hallucis longus, and peroneus longus 1/5; left side 4/5)

contradict_spans: lower‐extremity arteriography showed no significant vascular lesions
concepts.why: The patient's decreased ankle‐brachial indices suggest peripheral artery disease, but the lack of significant vascular lesions on arteriography contradicts this diagnosis.

The lack of significant vascular lesions on lower-extremity arteriography, combined with the progression of neurological symptoms such as foot drop and absent Achilles reflexes, suggests an alternative diagnosis to vascular disease.

rationales.F01: Initial presentation of numbness and pain in the right lower extremity is non-specific.
rationales.F02: Muscle weakness in the right tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus suggests peroneal nerve involvement.
rationales.F05: Positive straight-leg-raising test suggests lumbar disc herniation.
rationales.F08: Lumbar MRI showing a right-sided disc herniation at L5-S1 supports the diagnosis of lumbar disc herniation.
rationales.F09: Abnormal peroneal-nerve conduction studies support the diagnosis of peroneal nerve palsy.
rationales.F10: Decreased ankle-brachial indices suggest possible peripheral artery disease.
rationales.F11: Absence of significant vascular lesions on lower-extremity arteriography rules out peripheral artery disease.
rationales.F12: Development of right foot drop with muscle weakness and absent Achilles reflexes suggests progression of peroneal nerve palsy and possible chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy.
